$schema-note: The mutant list, per unit, as data -- which is what closes Risk R13.
Every slice in the plan reports a mutation tally and none of them could be re-run: the mutants
were hand edits in a scratch worktree and were thrown away, so a tally was an assertion rather
than a measurement (Risk R13, plan section 6.145). A mutant here is a find/replace against one
ported file plus what it is EXPECTED to do, and `python tools/mutate.py` turns the tally back
into a command.
FIELDS.
unit.name     what to pass to --unit
unit.slice    the plan row this list belongs to
unit.filter   substrings handed to the test runner, one per TEST_CLASS that covers this
unit, so a mutant runs its own tests rather than the whole suite
unit.tests    how many tests those filters select, VERIFIED against the unmutated build
before any mutant is applied. A filter that selects the wrong tests reports
survivors for code it never ran, which is worse than no filter at all --
`hyperspace` was recorded as "Hyperspace" and matched three tests in other
files whose method names contain the word (plan section 6.147). The number
is a tripwire on the SELECTION, and the two directions do
not mean the same thing: a RISE is normally tests that did not exist when the
number was written, and is re-based here with the reason in the unit's note; a
FALL is a filter that has stopped reaching its own class, and is a bug
mutant.id     the name the plan uses for it, where the plan named one
mutant.find   text that must appear EXACTLY ONCE in the file; the run fails loudly if not,
because a mutant that silently applied nowhere is a mutant reported as caught
mutant.expect caught | survives | equivalent | uncompilable
mutant.selftest  true on the one mutant per unit whose job is to prove the HARNESS works --
an unmissable change the suite cannot fail to catch. A run in which a selftest
mutant survives is a run whose every other answer is worthless, and the tool
stops there rather than reporting a tally (Risk R13, plan section 6.119)
`expect: caught` is the normal case and anything else must say why in its note. A run fails
when an outcome differs from its expectation in EITHER direction: a new survivor is a gap in
the tests, and a recorded survivor that starts being caught is debt that has been paid and
should be written down as paid.
M6-b-8, 2026-09-09 -- EIGHTY-NINE OF NINETY-SEVEN MUTANTS DELETED, AND RULE 3 IS BROKEN ON PURPOSE.
Rule 3 of the plan says a mutant is re-anchored and never dropped. It cannot be honoured here.
M6-b-5 deleted the 337 tests that compared the port against the original, and the corpus was
built to measure THOSE tests. The owner ruled on 2026-09-09 to delete what no longer has
coverage rather than record it as an expected survivor, so that every mutant left is one the
suite is expected to catch and the corpus is a gate again.
IT WAS DONE IN TWO STEPS AND THE SECOND IS THE ONE THAT MATTERED. Eight units -- tactics,
hyperspace, trumbles, missions, rng, arith, planetdraw, spawn -- lost every TEST_CLASS their
filters named, which is 71 mutants and needs no run to establish. The remaining five units were
then RUN, because a unit whose filter still selects tests is not the same as a unit those tests
can still see: 18 of the 26 survived, including four of the five units' own selftests. `shipmove`
and `flight` had not one caught mutant left and went whole; `raster` kept five of nine and
`cloud-seed` one of seven.
THE SELFTESTS ARE THE FINDING. `ra-selftest` zeroed `nextRasterLine` -- a register the deleted
comparison read on every one of 256 passes and no surviving test reads at all. It survived, and
because a surviving selftest stops the run by design, the corpus could not be measured at all
until the flags were lifted for one pass. A unit's selftest has to be unmissable TO THE TESTS
THAT EXIST, and three of the four that failed were unmissable only to tests that had been
deleted three slices earlier.
WHAT THAT COSTS, SO THAT NOBODY READS A GREEN RUN AS MORE THAN IT IS. The corpus now says
something about four files -- Canvas.cpp, Raster.cpp, ShipDraw.cpp and Game.cpp -- and nothing
about the other thirteen it used to cover: Arith, Rng, ShipMove, Spawn, PlanetDraw, Flight,
FlightLoop, Tactics, Trumbles, Hyperspace, Missions and Commander.h. Those files are not less
covered than they were yesterday -- the tests went first and the mutants only measured them --
but the instrument that would have SAID SO is gone too. ADR-009 section 4 carries the same fact.
The floor went from fourteen files to three. M6-0-g chose fourteen on the argument that after
detachment a mutant is the only instrument that says whether a test would notice; the argument
still holds and the floor is simply what can be met. It was written never to shrink.
One recorded EQUIVALENT went with its unit: `sm-mltu2-carry`, whose proof was that `MLTU2`'s
carry into the middle byte is always clear at that point. The proof is in this file's history
and in the journal; it is not re-derivable from what is left.

units.name: raster
note: COMIRQ1's VIC-II half (plan section 6.155). Written with the slice, so this unit is a
measurement from its first run rather than a test of a reconstruction.
FOUR of the handler's six registers reach the screen and they are two effects. `moonflower`
and `welcome` are the energy bomb; `santana` and `lotus` are how the explosion sprite is kept
out of the dashboard, which is a colour change rather than a clip. The other two -- `shango`
and the memory pointers -- are programmed correctly and consumed by nothing, so only the
oracle's write-ORDER comparison can tell a right value from a wrong one there. That is why
the comparison is a sequence and not a final state.
`ra-blit-per-sprite` is the one mutant outside `Raster.cpp`, and it is here rather than in a
canvas unit because what it breaks is this routine's output being read per screen row.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN PROOF for this unit, since M6-b-8. `ra-selftest` was here and zeroed `nextRasterLine`, which the comparison against the original read on every one of 256 passes -- and which no surviving test reads at all, so it survived and stopped the run. This one is unmissable to the tests that are left: `innersec` is the only thing that moves `RASTCT`, and `TheSplitAlternates` asserts that two passes return it to where it started. Keep it first.

BIT BOMB / BPL reads bit 7 and nothing else. The sweep runs the bomb byte at 0, &80, &7F and &FF, and &7F is the one that tells this bit from any other: every bit but the top one set, and the flash must not start.

welcome,X, and which half reads which byte. Taking the fixed one for both halves means the space view never flashes -- the bomb's whole visible effect below the mode change -- and the oracle's VIC+&21 write says so on the pass the port got wrong.

INC welcome sits ABOVE the split test, so both passes reach it and the colour moves twice a frame. This mutant is the plausible mistake -- incrementing only on the pass that shows it -- and it halves the flash rate. Caught on the dashboard pass, where the oracle's welcome has moved and the port's has not.

Deciding a sprite's mode once instead of per screen row. The VIC-II decides it as it scans, which is why a burst that straddles the split is drawn on one side only; pinning the half to the space view's draws the whole thing over the dashboard. Re-anchored at Resolution.md RS-0, when `BlitSprite` took the output's split row as a parameter so that one blit serves the canvas and the 640x400 picture.

units.name: cloud-seed
note: The EE55 cloud seeding, the carries it reads and the two defects the tightened comparison
found beside it (plan section 6.157). Every decision here is a flag: which carry the first
DORND rolls in, what the other three get, what EE51 leaves, what ANGRY leaves, what the
scooped canister's roll gets. Each mutant flips one and names the oracle test that sees it.
THE COUNT WENT 17 -> 18 (M6-d-17): M6-a-1 added `TheFlightFrameShips.TheDockingChecksMatchISDK`
while closing the fourth coverage gap.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN PROOF for this unit, and the only mutant left in it (M6-b-8). Byte 2 is the vertex count `DOEXP` loops down from; zero is the unseeded value that wrote 250 bytes across the neighbouring heaps, and `TheWreckageStaysInsideTheSpaceView` bounds every exploding ship's heap by its blueprint's `heapBytes` on every frame of the death sequence. The other six cloud-seed mutants were caught only by comparisons against the original and were deleted with them.

units.name: game
note: `Elite::Game` (Modernize.md section 4.4) -- the object that calls the routines every other unit
compares. Nothing here is arithmetic; what a mutant catches is a CALL left out, which is the shape
of every outer-loop defect the plan's section 6.128 and 6.111 record: a routine ported, swept, green
and reached by nothing. InputTimer.md T-2 added the first, on the docked pass reaching `MLOOP`'s
part 5 whole rather than its two countdowns alone.

mutants.find:
PressKey(_key); // `thiskey`, which is zero when nothing is held
    return syncs;
mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN OracleIsPresent for this unit. A docked pass that never dispatches its key never ticks TT107's countdown, and ADockedPassWithNoKeyStillRunsTheCountdown reads the counter. Keep it first.

mutants.find: const std::uint8_t syncs = RunLoopTail(m_universe, m_ports, m_universe.commander, m_universe.options.authorNames, false); // docked
mutants.note: The docked pass back to its two countdowns, which is what the port ran until T-2. ADockedPassBreedsTheTrumblesAndAsksForItsSyncs reads the hold after sixty-four passes and the syncs a chart asks for with the names on. Would have hidden: a hold that stops breeding at the airlock, and a docked pace priced from a constant rather than from the gate.
